body:
This worries me a bit about the feature's usability in complex projects. A common complaint about Godot is that various systems' behavior vary too much between debug and release builds. In fact, people have started to look into reducing the differences in 4.x to make project exporting more reliable. This is especially important as many people rely on stack traces in 4.x, which can be enabled in projects exported in release mode too (e.g. for automated exception reporting).

To resolve this, we'll probably need some kind of source map system so that line numbers can be traced back to the original source, and displayed to the user in a transparent manner. This is what CSS and JavaScript do when minified. If optimization is moved to export-time, then the source maps will also have to be included in the exported PCK.

body:
> To resolve this, we'll probably need some kind of source map system so that line numbers can be traced back to the original source, and displayed to the user in a transparent manner.

The PR already does this. Sometimes there won't be an exact match, but it should give ballpark from the original source.

The same issue is more obvious when stepping through optimized code in the Godot IDE, where it can jump around in the source a bit (the same occurs when debugging optimized c++ in any programming IDE).

> This worries me a bit about the feature's usability in complex projects. A common complaint about Godot is that various systems' behavior vary too much between debug and release builds.

With debug / release optimization in programming in all languages, the aim is to (as much as possible) have the effects be 1:1 in debug and release. If there is a regression between the two it is an engine bug to be fixed (rather than a bug in user code). Typically there are some optional allowances typically made when optimizing like "assuming no aliasing" switches etc, but this GDScript optimizer is very conservative.

Optimization here is optional, it can be turned off in exports (and is off by default), so users can:

* Ship non-optimized GDScript only (default, same as before)
* Ship two builds, optimized / non-optimized (for debugging)
* Ship only optimized build (after testing)

Also bear in mind important point - only some GDScript intensive games / apps will benefit. If you are not e.g. using tight loops in GDScript, and are using simple scripts with short functions such that most time is spent in c++, there won't be much gains on the table. But if you are e.g. making a chess game with lots of intensive calculations, having the ability to optimize offers the potential to make the game a *lot* faster.

In all cases, code optimization is a trade-off (this will apply in 4.x too, when that eventually gets optimization). You can either play it safe, and have slow performance, or you work through teething issues to get best performance possible.

This is more a philosophical question - it is what is it, and it depends how much we care about offering users good performance. We get a lot of regular requests / complaints to make `GDScript` faster. Making modules / GDExtensions works as an alternative, but is a step too far for many users, and many would prefer an intermediate solution that was easy for them to use.
